Product description
Description and operation of the software control for the treatment table system
• Part 132 - slow down point, at which speed is limited and deceleration occurs.
• Part 141 - position gain, which determines the accuracy of the positioning.
There are also three parts that have an effect on the performance when small movements are
made:
• Part 135 - threshold, at which ASU correction starts.
• Part 142 - ASU increment gain, the increment value of each ASU correction.
• Part 140 - deadband, the positional error value at which ASU correction starts.
Slow down point
Part 132 sets a distance value to the last position of the movement. At the set distance, the
maximum speed is decreased to make sure that the system decelerates. If the value of Part 132 is
increased, deceleration occurs earlier. Because of IEC requirements, the value of Part 132 must
not be decreased below the default value.
Position gain
Part 141 sets the gain of the servo and therefore determines the accuracy of the positioning. If
the value of Part 141 is too high, the movement tends to oscillate about the required positional
setting, so the value of Part 141 should be such that it does not oscillate or overshoot by an
unacceptable amount.
If the movement undershoots, the value of Part 141 should be increased. If the movement
overshoots or oscillates, the value of Part 141 should be reduced. The performance may be
different in the two directions, so it may be necessary to compromise between undershoot in
one direction and overshoot in the other.
Part 132 and Part 141 can both be used to prevent oscillation, but their effects are subtly
different. Part 141 has most effect close to the final position because, for larger errors, the speed
is limited by the speed limits or by the slow down position. In general, the value of Part 141
should be reduced only if it is not possible to prevent overshoot/oscillation by reasonable
adjustment of Part 132.
It may be advisable to disable the nudging facility while determining the optimum values for Part
132 and Part 141.
Threshold
Part 135 applies a starting correction so that the ASU correction does not start from zero, thus
reducing the time taken to reach the correction that causes movement. Part 135 has a range of 0
to 50.
ASU increment gain
For small movements, the positional correction may not provide sufficient drive to allow the
motor to overcome stiction. If no movement is detected, an ASU correction (process_param_7 of
the servo item) is applied. The ASU correction is incremented by Part 142 at each occurrence of
the host machine control system loop (every 120 ms), until movement occurs when the ASU
correction is reset to zero.
The ASU correction applies a series of nudges which move the treatment table to the desired
position. Since the amount of correction reduces as the movement nears the desired position,
the amplitude of the ASU correction to cause movement increases. The ASU correction thus
forms a sawtooth waveform of increasing amplitude.
Part 142 has a range of 0 to 5.
Deadband
ASU correction is not applied unless the positional error is greater than the value of Part 140.
This can be used to prevent small oscillations about the desired position, but will reduce the
accuracy of positioning. Part 140 has a range of 0 to 10. If the ASU_correction is plotted (using
the graphing facility) against time while holding down the PSS ASU buttons for about 10 to

3.29.3 Description of the XVI table factors
If the treatment table is installed on a digital accelerator with X-Ray Volume Imaging (XVI) system
R3.5 or later, and the treatment table has been re-calibrated, then the XVI table factors must be

the gantry or the treatment table. The software for the digital accelerator does not automatically
send this changed calibration data to the XVI software. This causes errors to occur when XVI
calculates the table correction values, because the calibration data does not agree.
Therefore, it is important that you use the XVI DCB utility in the XVI software to copy the
applicable changed calibration data to the XVI software.

4.1.8 Using the manual crank handle
If there are no motorized movements, operate the manual crank handle to lift or lower the
treatment table.
1 Lower the bellows cover.
2 Attach the manual crank handle to the output shaft of the height motor.
001898 ©2013 Elekta Limited
Figure 4.17 Manual crank handle on the height motor shaft.
3 Release the height motor brake. Follow one of these two procedures.
a Use the brake release tool.
b Attach a length of string or wire to the brake release handle.
4 Pull the string or wire away from the brake release handle and along the axis of the height
motor.
5 Turn the manual crank handle clockwise to lift the treatment table, or counterclockwise to
lower the treatment table.
Note: 800 turns of the crank handle is approximately equal to 1000 mm of movement.
6 When the treatment table is in position, disengage the manual crank handle from the shaft
of the height motor.
Note: 800 turns of the crank handle is approximately equal to 1000 mm of movement.
WARNING 4.4
Do not use motorized movement of the treatment table until after you remove the manual
crank handle. If you ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury.
7 If you used a string or wire to release the brake, remove these from the brake release
handle.

5.10.3 Adjusting the microswitch PCB on the column indent mechanism
If the treatment table is not at 0°, the buzzer PCB activates and makes a sound.
Note: You must make sure that the microswitch PCB is set up correctly and in specification before
clinical operation.
The audible indication stops approximately ±5° from the 0° indent position. For example, when
you rotate the column to 0°, you hear a sound when you are approximately ±5° away from 0°.
This stops when in the 0° indent position. Equally, if you rotate the column away from 0°, you
hear a sound when the column is at approximately ±5°. After ±5°, the sound stops.
Note: It is important that the treatment table is set up correctly on the inner edge (2) to give an audible
indication at 0.13° (see Figure 5.62).
1 Attach the column indent alignment template to the G-end of the treatment table.
2 Make sure that the projection of the crosswire image aligns with the crosswires on the
template.

5.11.2 Installing the service end stops on the longitudinal carriage
assembly
The installation of the service end stops lets the longitudinal carriage assembly move more than
its usual range of movement in the G-direction. This gives full access to the longitudinal drive
mechanism and brake units, and it prevents the separation of the longitudinal carriage assembly
from the treatment table.
CAUTION 5.8
Do not move the lateral or longitudinal carriage assembly more than its usual range of
movement because some of the roller bearings can disengage from the bearing channels. If you
ignore this caution, you can cause damage to the equipment.

Prerequisites

5.17.2 Installing the service end stops on the lateral carriage assembly
The installation of the service end stops lets the lateral carriage assembly move more than its
usual range of movement in the B-direction. This gives full access to the lateral drive mechanism
and brake units on the A-side of the lateral carriage assembly. This prevents the separation of the
lateral carriage assembly from the treatment table.
CAUTION 5.9
Do not move the lateral or longitudinal carriage assembly more than its usual range of

5.20.2 Installing a potentiometer in the lateral movement system
Prerequisites
Digital voltmeter.
1 Move the lateral drive plate to the center position, and align the holes in the lateral drive
plate with the holes in the lateral drive subassembly.
2 Install two screws to lock the lateral drive plate in position.
3 At PCB835, connect the cable to the applicable plug:
– PL3 (lateral movement coarse potentiometer)
– PL4 (lateral movement fine potentiometer)
– PL5 (lateral movement check potentiometer).
4 Adjust the new potentiometer until the voltage is equal to 5 V (±10 mV).
5 Put the potentiometer in position and install the nut and washer to attach the
potentiometer to the bracket.
Note: Do not fully tighten the nut.
6 Apply a small quantity of Loctite® 243™ to the threads of the set screw, and tighten the set
screw on the shaft of the potentiometer.
7 Measure the voltage of the coarse or check potentiometer between pin 1 and 2.
8 Rotate the drive gear of the new potentiometer to adjust the measured voltage until it is
equal to 5 V (±10 mV).
Note: For a new fine potentiometer, you do not have to adjust the voltage.
9 Tighten the 13mm nut and make sure that the voltage is equal to 5 V (±10 mV).
10 Remove the two screws that lock the lateral drive plate in position.
11 Install the longitudinal drive subassembly.
12 Remove the safety support struct.
13 Assemble the longitudinal carriage assembly.
14 Do the calibration of the longitudinal movement system.

5.31 Adjusting the height movement limit switches
5.31.1 Adjusting the upper limit switches of the height movement
mechanism
There are four limit switches and four adjustable actuators (two of each for the lower limit, and
the upper limit) installed on the height mechanism. The table top must be installed when you set
up the upper and lower limit switches.
1 Set the column rotation to 0°.
2 Lower the bellows cover.
3 Attach a length of string or wire to the brake release handle of the height motor, this will let
you manually release the brake.
4 On the user interface module, operate the HEIGHT thumbwheel to move the treatment
table up, until you can get access to the upper limit microswitches.
Note: The upper limit microswitches are on the gun side of the upper arm assembly.

supply

WARNING 5.14

the electrical supply before you start the work. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal
injury.

supply. There are high voltages at the UPS, although the electrical supply to the EIM cabinet is
disconnected. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury.

cabinet.

the PSU.

the PSU.
On the front panel of the EIM PSU, the amber lamp below CB1 goes off.
3 On the interface cabinet, switch CB13 to OFF to disconnect the electrical supply to the UPS.

5.38.3 Examining the operation of the emergency down drive
1 Start the digital accelerator to supply the 24VACHOST signal to the EIM cabinet.
2 Set the digital accelerator to the Preparatory machine state.
3 Move the treatment table to its highest position.
4 Operate the EMERGENCY STOP button in the treatment room wall to simulate a failure to
the electrical power supply.
This removes the electrical power supply and the 24VACHOST signal from the EIM cabinet.
5 Make sure that the operation of the ENABLE bar on each user interface module causes the
treatment table to move down.
6 After six minutes:
a Make sure that the LEDs in the buttons of each user interface module stay on.
This shows that the UPS has not shut down and the UPS battery is in a good condition.
b Make sure that the ENABLE bar of each user interface module causes the treatment
table to move down.
7 Reset the EMERGENCY STOP button in the treatment room.
This switches on the electrical power supply and supplies the 24VACHOST signal to the EIM
cabient.
8 Set the digital accelerator to the Preparatory machine state.
9 At the TCS, do a system shutdown.
This removes the electrical power supply to the EIM cabinet, but continues to supply the
24VACHOST signal.
10 Make sure that the LEDs in the buttons of each user interface module go off.
– If the EDD Timer Module is installed (machines before Serial No. 152531), the UPS shuts
down after approximately 5 minutes (±1 minute). If necessary, you can adjust this time
at the EDD timer module.
– If the EDD Timer Module is not installed (machines from Serial No. 152531), the UPS
shuts down after approximately 1 minute (±30 seconds).

5.41.12 Fine-tuning the treatment table movement
5.41.12.1 Description of fine-tuning the movement servos of the treatment table
This is a description of the the sequence to fine-tune the movement servos of the treatment
table. These procedures are applicable for Integrity™ TCS, with triple potentiometers.
The procedures to fine-tune the movement servos of the treatment table are applicable for all
the movement systems, which are the:
• Longitudinal
• Lateral
• Height
• Iso-rotation.
Fine-tune the movement servos of all the movement systems from the control room. Use the
CCTV cameras in the treatment room to see the effect of the adjustments on the treatment
table. Remove all the unwanted equipment near the treatment table before you do the
procedures.
The procedures tune the parameters of each movement servo in the sequence that follows:
• The slow down point and position gain parameters
• The threshold parameter
• The acceleration limit parameter
• The ASU increment and deadband parameters.

5.41.12.8 Fine-tuning the ASU increment
This is the procedure to examine the service graph and fine-tune the ASU increment on a
movement servo on the treatment table. This is the applicable procedure for Integrity™ TCS with
triple potentiometers.
1 Examine the service graph. (This is for Part 137 only).
Note: Part 142 (which is usually set to 1) has an effect on the slope of the saw-tooth plot. If the value of
Part 142 increases, the slope of the sawtooth line increases, and the time between nudges
decreases. A value of 0 disables the nudge function.
2 Set Part 142 to the lowest value (usually 2). This will let the treatment table move to the
necessary position in 6 to 8 seconds.
3 If the treatment table is not in the necessary position in 6 to 8 seconds, you must make an
adjustment:
a To decrease the time for the treatment table to move to the necessary position,
increase the value of Part 142. It has a maximum value of 5.
b If the value of Part 142 is too high, it is possible that the treatment table will oscillate or
go through the set position (the correction intermittently changes from positive to
negative). If this occurs, decrease the value of Part 142 by 1 or 2 from its current
setting.
4 Continue to adjust the ASU increment and deadband until the ASU is stable, with no
oscillation and in a time between 6 and 8 seconds.

6.3.3 Elements of a signal name
Signal names have three elements:
• The first three letters of the signal name identify the item being driven by the signal.
• The next letter identifies the movement axis.
• The next three letters identify the source of the signal.
A line (bar) immediately above the name of a digital signal is an indication that the signal is
active-low (logic 0). For example:
MBKXYLTU
The names of digital signals that do not have a line (bar) immediately above the name are activehigh (logic 1).

1.4.4 Safety precautions for the electromagnetic compatibility
These are safety precautions to prevent an unwanted effect on the operation of the equipment by
the radio frequency emissions.
The design and manufacture of Elekta products is in compliance with applicable EMC standards.
The intended result of the standards is to minimize the risk of electromagnetic interference by RF
devices. The type of device and the distance to the equipment has an effect on the intensity of the
electromagnetic interference. The equipment includes the linear accelerator and accessories, the
control cabinets, the computers in the control room, and equipment from other manufacturer.
It is necessary to have special precautions for EMC emissions. Elekta recommends that you obey
these precautions when you use RF devices near the equipment.
• Do not use RF devices unless they are in compliance with international standards for
electromagnetic compatibility, for example, the CE or FCC mark.
• Do not use a two-way emergency radio in the treatment room or the control room. Only
use an emergency radio if there is an emergency.
• Do not use cellular telephones, or other devices with cellular modems near the
equipment. The Instructions for Use contains information on the minimum safe distance
of these devices from the equipment.
• When you use a device that is enabled for wireless operation, it must be a minimum of
10 cm from the equipment.
• Radio-Frequency Identification (RFID) readers, when activated to do a scan of a RFID tag,
must be a minimum of one meter from the equipment.
Note: The RFID systems that Elekta supply use lower power levels. You can safely use these RFID systems
when you obey the procedures in the Instructions for Use for the product.
The system must be installed, put into service, and maintained in compliance with the EMC
information in the Instructions for Use.
Contact Elekta for information about the compatibility of parts and equipment.
WARNING1.4
Do not put portable or mobile radio frequency (RF) communication devices near to
the equipment. The emissions from such RF devices can be more than the EMC
standards, and can have unwanted effects on the equipment operation. If you
ignore this warning, the RF emissions can cause the equipment to have a
malfunction. A malfunction can cause fatal injury, clinical mistreatment, or damage
to the equipment.
WARNING1.5

They can have an effect on the EMC performance, which can increase EMC
emissions or decrease the immunity to RF interference of the equipment. If you
ignore this warning, incorrect radiation delivery and other malfunctions can occur,
which can cause fatal injury or clinical mistreatment.

1.4.34 Expected service life of the equipment
The expected service life is the length of time that the regular service and repair procedures can keep
the equipment safe to operate.
WARNING1.37
Do not operate the equipment unless you correctly complete the safety checks,
planned maintenance schedules, and extended life checks. If you ignore this
warning, you can cause fatal injury and damage to the equipment.
The expected service life of this equipment is 15 years of normal use.
The Elekta definition for 'expected service life' is the length of time that the regular service and
repair procedures can keep the equipment safe to operate.
The Elekta definition of 'normal use' is the treatment of 50 patients each day for five days each
week of the year.
The level of operation of the equipment can be different to ‘normal use’. This has an effect on the
length of the service life. Because of wear of parts, the risk of a malfunction can increase after 10
years operation. Elekta recommends that before you continue operation after 10 years, you
complete the regular extended life checks.
Elekta can help the User with the correct safety checks, planned maintenance schedules, and the
regular extended life checks for continued safe operation of the equipment.
The system must be maintained throughout its expected service life in compliance with the EMC
information detailed in the appendix in this document.
For information on the above checks and schedules, contact your local Elekta representative.
1.4.35 Disposal of the equipment
This is the procedure for the disposal of the equipment at End of Life to prevent damage to health
and the environment by radioactive and hazardous material.
WARNING1.38
Do not discard radioactive and hazardous material through the domestic waste
systems or in the environment. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury
and damage to the environment.
End of life (EOL) disposal is the procedure to disassemble, remove, and discard the equipment, in
full or in parts, to a condition where it is not possible to operate the equipment for its intended
use.
Always use procedures that give the best possible protection to the environment when you
remove and discard the equipment. The procedures must obey the laws and regulations of the
jurisdictions in which you discard the equipment. Do not discard Elekta equipment through the
domestic waste systems.
Only a Qualified Expert (QE) and an approved facility with an applicable license, must remove and
discard the equipment and recycle the material. Do not discard material that is hazardous to
health and the environment together with other material.
Before you remove and discard equipment, contact Elekta for information.

3.2 Navigating the linear accelerator corrective maintenance

This Linear Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual has been designed in a modular format
that will eventually comprise a fully integrated, electronically published suite of information. The
main characteristics of modular documentation are that:
• Where possible, a piece of information resides in one place only - it is not duplicated and
is therefore easy to update.
• Categories of information (for example, repair instructions) always appear at the same
place in each module - so the information is easy to find.
• Cross-references are used to direct users to associated and/or more detailed
information.
The Linear Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual set therefore comprises a number of
modules, each of which is dedicated to a primary system of the linear accelerator. The modules are
compiled into three volumes as listed in Table3.1.

With the exception of this reference module, each module of the Linear Accelerator Corrective

3.3 Safety information for service personnel
This section presents the complex safety issues that apply when an Elekta linear accelerator is
serviced. Warnings of specific hazards also appear at the appropriate point of application
throughout the entire Linear Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual set.
3.3.1 General safety
The linear accelerator is Class 1, Type B equipment according to IEC 60601-2-1, Part2C, Computer
Controlled Radiotherapy Equipment.
To make sure that all service personnel work in a safe way, all warnings and cautions throughout
the Linear Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual must be strictly obeyed.
The use of this equipment should be controlled by qualified members of the hospital staff, whose
responsibilities include:
The assignment of passwords to suitable persons for each of the various levels of
authorization.
Making sure that all persons who work on the linear accelerator are competent to perform
the procedures for which they are authorized.
The equipment should be used only by service personnel who are trained in the use of locally
applicable regulations, standards and laws that govern the safe use of ionizing radiation, and in the
specific use of this equipment.
Service personnel must be familiar with the contents of this document before attempting any
procedure and/or instruction given in the Linear Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual set.
Service personnel must use the equipment only as described in this manual, and be aware of all
warnings given in this manual.
Elekta provides training courses for service personnel, which cover the safe use of this equipment.
The members of the hospital staff who control the use of the linear accelerator must arrange for
the regular maintenance of the equipment as stated in the operation and service manuals.
3.3.2 Powering up and powering down the linear accelerator
3.3.2.1 Emergency switches
Service personnel must be thoroughly familiar with the location and function of all emergency
switches associated with the linear accelerator. These include:
• The STOP button on the handheld controller(s) in the treatment room.
• The emergency stop motors button on each user interface of the treatment table in the
treatment room.
• All locally installed emergency power OFF switches in the treatment room, the control
room and the equipment room.
3.3.2.2 Powering up and powering down the linear accelerator
Usually, each hospital has a local procedure for powering up and powering down an Elekta linear
accelerator and, if so, the local procedure should always be used. In the absence of local
procedures, follow the instructions given in the applicable manual of Instructions for User - Service
Mode for the TCS.

3.3.3 Fire hazards
WARNING3.1
There continues to be a risk of high voltage electric shock after the power supply
switch of the equipment is put in the OFF position. Some of the customer interfaces
can continue to supply electrical power to the electrical terminals. This can give you
a high voltage electric shock. If you ignore this warning, a high voltage electric
shock can cause fatal injury.
Make sure that all equipment that supplies oxygen to patients is switched Off and does not leak
during service and repair activities.
3.3.3.1 Action in the event of a fire
WARNING3.2
Fire regulations applicable to the medical area in use must be rigorously observed
and enforced.
Fire extinguishers suitable to fight electrical and non-electrical fires must be
provided. These fire extinguishers must be clearly and correctly labelled, and must
be sited for maximum access and ease of use.
The fire extinguishers must be properly maintained in accordance with the
manufacturer’s servicing and maintenance schedule.
Failure to observe these precautions can cause fatal injury.
WARNING3.3
On electrical or chemical fires, use only extinguishers that are specifically labelled
for the purpose.
The use of water or other liquids on an electrical fire can lead to fatal injury.
When it is safe to do so, isolate the linear accelerator from its electrical supply before attempting
to fight a fire. This will reduce the risk of electric shocks.
3.3.4 Hazards to service personnel
WARNING3.4
The linear accelerator is potentially hazardous.
The risks to the health and safety of all persons in the vicinity of the machine
include ionizing radiation and heavy moving masses.
Additional hazards to service personnel when the covers of the equipment are
removed include exposure to radioactivity, electric shock and inhalation of toxic
materials.
When performing the procedures described in this manual, service personnel may be exposed to
three, potentially life-threatening hazards:
• Induced radioactivity (see Section3.3.5)
• High voltages (see Section3.3.6)
• Toxic materials (see Section3.3.7)
Safe methods of working are described in the text. The information given in warning notices,
together with the appropriate instructions, must be read and strictly obeyed.

3.3.5.1 Safe working practices
WARNING3.5
Incorrect work practices present an ionizing radiation hazard to any person in the
vicinity of the linear accelerator.
All personnel who service or operate the linear accelerator must:

3.4 Elekta linear accelerators
Elekta linear accelerators are machines for use in clinical radiation therapy. They produce a beam
of high energy particles that is accurately delivered to the target tumor in a patient reclining on a
treatment table. A high tension (HT) and radio frequency (RF) source provides the energy that
accelerates the particles. Travelling wave technology is used to transport the radiation beam, and a
beam limiting device (BLD) with collimation is used to shape the beam and deliver it precisely to
the target.
The linear accelerator is a drum and gantry structure that rotates through 360° around an
isocentric axis. The components that produce the radiation beam are mounted on the drum and
the gantry. The machine is the main component in a complete system for the delivery of
therapeutic radiation to patients. The other parts of the system are:
• Treatment table
• Beam limiting device (BLD)
• Control system
• Imaging systems.
The linear accelerator is usually installed in a suite of three rooms which contain the following
main parts:
• Treatment room - gantry, BLD, treatment table, monitors, handheld controllers, imaging
system components, covers, wall-mounted lasers.
• Control room - linear accelerator control system, function keypad, imaging system
workstations.
• Equipment room - gantry drum and all other equipment such as the interface cabinet,
reeling post, gas cylinder, table electrical interface module (EIM), client’s interface
terminal board (CITB) and so on.

systems are not topics in this Digital Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual but are fully
described in dedicated document sets.
3.4.5 Clinical beams
The digital accelerator generates two types of clinical beam:
• Electron - used to treat superficial tumors (less than 5 cm deep). The therapeutic energy
range for electrons is 4MeV to 22 MeV.
• X-ray (photon) - used to treat deep-seated tumors. The therapeutic energy range of
X-rays is 4 MV to 25 MV. Typically, X-ray beams are used in combinations (for example,
opposed pairs), which deliver very high doses to the target, but with relatively low skin
doses. X-ray beams provide up to three energy levels.

3.5 Brief description of the digital accelerator assembly
The digital accelerator itself comprises the following main assemblies:
• Gantry drum
• Gantry arm
• Interface cabinet
• Cable reeling post.
Gantry drum
The gantry drum is housed in the equipment room. Subunits of the digital accelerator are mounted
in dedicated areas within the gantry drum and at the rear of the gantry drum.
Gantry arm
The gantry arm projects from the gantry drum into the treatment room. The arm contains the
linear accelerating waveguide that transports the radiation beam from its source in the gantry
drum to the BLD mounted at the treatment end of the gantry arm.
Interface cabinet
The interface cabinet is located in the equipment room. It provides the electrical interconnection
between all the systems and subsystems of the digital accelerator.
Cable reeling post
The cable reeling post is located in the equipment room. It feeds and retracts the main cable loom
to and from the gantry drum as the drum rotates. The reeling post also provides connections to
external services such as cooling water and dielectric gas.

3.5.1 Principle of operation
An Elekta digital accelerator comprises a number of primary systems:
• HT and RF
• Beam physics
• Power supplies and Interlocks
• Dosimetry
• Movements

3.5.1.1 HT and RF systems
The HT and RF systems operating together produce a radiation beam of high-energy electrons or
X-rays (photons).
Stable, high-voltage pulses are produced by the HT system. In the RF system, the HT pulses cause
the generation of a travelling RF wave that is used to transport electrons through an accelerating
waveguide and into the BLD.
The travelling RF wave is produced by a modulator that is powered by the high-voltage pulses from
the HT system. A magnetron in the modulator generates an oscillating RF power input to the
waveguide and thus forms the travelling RF wave. An electron gun, powered by the same HT
pulses as the magnetron, injects electrons into the waveguide where they are transported by the
RF wave.
The compact design of the digital accelerator is made possible by the use of the high-power
magnetron as the RF power source.
See Digital Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual - High Tension and Radio Frequency
Systems for a full description of the HT and RF systems.
3.5.1.2 Beam physics system
The RF energy is propagated along the accelerating waveguide as travelling waves. Energy is
transferred from the travelling waves to the electrons, which are thus accelerated to emerge at the
output of the waveguide with considerable gain in energy. The travelling waves of RF and electron
energy are transported along their path by a set of magnets that surround the accelerating
waveguide.
The high-energy electron beam passes through an achromatic bending magnet system that
deflects the beam through different angles until it finally emerges at the target/window. Here the
beam strikes a target that generates X-rays, or passes through a thin metal window to produce
electron radiation. Beyond the target/window area, the radiation beam passes to the BLD.
See Digital Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual - Beam Physics System for a full
description of the beam physics system.

3.5.1.3 Power supplies and Interlocks
Power supplies
The digital accelerator requires electrical power supplies for a number of systems and subsystems:
• Main three-phase supply for the HT and other systems
• Low voltage (LV) power supplies for various magnet solenoids such as the Magnetron
magnet, the focus coils and the coarse and fine bending magnets
• Low tension (LT) power supplies for the control areas and motor drive areas
• Interlock system power supplies.
Three-phase electrical power is obtained from the hospital main supply. The separate power
supplies for the magnet solenoids are produced by the low voltage power supply unit (LVPSU)
assembly. The control areas, the motor drive areas and the interlock system relays are supplied by
local power supply units.
Interlock system
The digital accelerator is potentially hazardous. To protect patients, clinical staff, service
technicians and others in the vicinity of the machine, a number of hardware, firmware and
software interlocks are fitted.
The principle of operation of all the interlock chains is similar. The hardware of each chain is a
serial circuit consisting of relays, contactors and PCBs in all three control areas. The inputs to the
interlock chains come from the TCC (software interlocks), from local PCB programming (firmware
interlocks), and from sensing devices such as temperature and pressure switches.
Each input imposes one or more operating or safety conditions on its respective interlock chain. If
any condition is violated, the affected interlock chain is broken and the operation of the digital
accelerator is partially or entirely inhibited while the unsafe condition prevails.
There are six hardware interlock chains:
• Main
• Low tension (LT)
• Movements
• HT
• Pulse repetition frequency (PRF)
• Client.
With the exception of the PRF interlock, the hardware interlocks all control the contactors which
supply mains electrical power to different systems and subsystems of the digital accelerator. The
PRF interlock system directly inhibits the generation of radiation if an unsafe condition occurs.
The HT, movements and PRF interlocks all have dual circuits (primary and secondary).
See Digital Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual - Power Supplies and Interlock Systems for
a full description of the power supplies and interlocks.
3.5.1.4 Dosimetry system
The dosimetry system controls and monitors the radiation dose delivered by the digital
accelerator. It also monitors the ambient temperature and atmospheric pressure during
treatment. All three measurements are made by dual circuits (channel A and channel B), and the
readings are compared by the TCC. A number of dosimetry interlocks prevent the delivery of
radiation in the event of a fault or error.
Radiation is detected by an ionization (ion) chamber in the path of the radiation beam, which feeds
data to both dosimetry channels. The system includes an arrangement to monitor the flatness of
the radiation field, and these signals provide software supervision of the beam control servos.

3.5.1.5 Movement systems
The moving assemblies discussed in this manual are the gantry of the digital accelerator and the
BLD. With the exception of rotation, other movements of the BLD are discussed in Corrective
Maintenance Manuals for Beam Limiting Devices.
The treatment table movement system is described in the Precise Treatment Table Corrective
Maintenance Manual.
The gantry has a dedicated movement system that controls the rotation of the gantry drum. The
BLD has a dedicated movement system that controls the rotation of the entire assembly. These are
known collectively as machine movements.
The principle of operation of each movement system is essentially the same. The moving assembly
is driven by one or more electric motors. The demand for a movement is given by the user at a
manual controller. The movement is enabled, and its speed and direction are set by the TCC. These
commands are processed in the respective control areas and motor drive areas of the digital
accelerator to provide drive signals to the appropriate motor.
Encoders monitor the actual position of the moving assembly, and a servo loop returns this
information to the TCC, which can therefore start and stop the movement, and dynamically adjust
the speed and direction of motion in real time. The positional data is also used by the TCC to
prevent the assembly from being driven beyond predetermined limits.
See Digital Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual - Movement Systems for a full description
of the movements system.
3.5.1.6 Cooling, gas and vacuum systems
Various components of the digital accelerator operate at high temperatures. The machine is
therefore equipped with a cooling water system comprising:
An external (primary) water circuit that receives cold water from, and returns warm water to,
the hospital’s water facility
An internal (secondary) water circuit - a closed loop with a heat exchanger that transfers heat
to the external return circuit.
The dielectric gas is used to cool the magnetron and waveguide windows and prevent arcing in the
rectangular section of the waveguide. The gas supply is obtained from a conventional cylinder
located in or near the reeling post.
The accelerating waveguide is evacuated to make sure that electrons are not obstructed or
deflected by collisions with gas molecules. The vacuum is maintained by two ion pumps - one at
the gun end of the waveguide and the other at the target end.
See Digital Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual - Cooling, Gas and Vacuum Systems for full
descriptions of the cooling, gas and vacuum systems.
3.5.1.7 System communications
The digital accelerator is controlled by the software that resides in the TCC, and the TCC
communicates with the digital accelerator via two serial links (A and B). At the digital accelerator,
the serial links connect to three separate control areas:
Radiation head (BLD) control area (RHCA)
HT control area (HTCA)
Interface cabinet control area (ICCA).

The control areas distribute command and data signals from the TCC to the other systems of the
digital accelerator, and return data and other information to the TCC. These signals are known as
items.
Each control area consists of a PCB rack with a backplane and a set of PCBs, and is divided into two
remote terminal units (RTU A and RTU B). Each RTU has integral power supplies, so that the
interlocks and safety circuits handled by each RTU operate independently.
Within each control area, the two RTUs communicate with each other over a dedicated bus. The
backplane provides the interconnection between the control areas and the other systems of the
digital accelerator.
See Digital Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual - System Communications for a full
description of the system communications.
3.5.1.8 Covers
All digital accelerators are fitted with a set of fiberglass covers which:
• Protect patients and operators from hazardous components and conditions within the
gantry arm and the BLD
• Protect the components of the digital accelerator in the treatment room from
inadvertent damage in use
• Present a pleasing and unthreatening aspect to patients in the treatment room.
Covers, and a supporting frame, provide the dividing wall between the treatment room and the
equipment room. Within the treatment room, the gantry arm of the digital accelerator is entirely
covered and, except for the treatment field, the BLD is also covered.
The cover sets for the digital accelerators are different in construction and color. See Digital
Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual - Covers for more information.
3.5.1.9 Accessories
The usual accessories supplied with Elekta digital accelerators are:
• Applicators
• Shadow trays
• Front pointer
• Optical distance meter.
Applicators are attached to the BLD when required by the prescription. They are used with
electron beam treatments to attain a uniform, sharply-defined field of the required dimensions.
Shadow trays are used with X-ray treatments to position blocks in the treatment field. This
provides final beam shaping and enables the safe delivery of irregularly shaped fields.
The front pointer is a mechanical assembly that attaches to an accessory ring on the BLD. It
indicates the isocenter of the radiation beam.
The optical distance meter is attached beneath the gantry arm. The device projects a scale that
indicate the source-to-surface distance (SSD) over a defined range.
See Digital Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual - Accessories for a full description of the
digital accelerator accessories.

3.7 Machine states
The digital accelerator can exist in a limited number of stable states only. Each state defines the
number of systems to which electrical power is applied. The higher the machine state, the greater
the number of systems that are powered up.
The switching of electrical power to the systems is accomplished via the hardware interlock chains,
which have software and firmware inputs. Each interlock chain applies power to a number of
circuits.
A flat interlock structure is used - as distinct from a tree structure. The flat structure employs a
small number of interlock chains that pass through each control area, with numerous relay
contacts and monitoring points.
Control of the interlock system is based on a 'state of readiness' regime in which the digital
accelerator occupies one of a relatively small number of states (known as a superstate). In each
superstate, a fixed hardware state is imposed on the remote terminal units (RTUs) in each control
area - for example, the appropriate contactors are enabled. This imposed condition is known as
the global state. Firmware on certain PCBs in each control area receives a global state code from
the TCC, which sets the global state of the addressed RTU.
The digital accelerator changes state automatically during power up, and normally waits in the
Preparatory state. If the software detects an error condition, the state of the digital accelerator
suspends to a lower level to prevent damage to the machine, or risk to the user or patient.
Users can force the digital accelerator to change certain states. See Instructions for Use - Service
Mode for the TCS for information on displaying the machine states and forcing the user-selectable
states.

4.5 Interface cabinet interlock assembly
The interlock assembly that occupies Area 74 in the interface cabinet is part of the interlock
system of the linear accelerator. The assembly houses a PCB rack containing interlock relay PCBs
IRC-74A, IRC-74B and IRC-74C and six 15-way connectors.
The arrangement of Area 74 is shown in the Linear Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual Power Supplies and Interlock Systems.
The IRC PCBs are described in Linear Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual - Power Supplies
and Interlock Systems.
4.6 Gantry base motor drive PSUs
The gantry base motor drive PSUs that occupies Area 75 of the interface cabinet are part of the
movement system, where they are used to power the motors that rotate the gantry. The area
contains two separate PSUs, each of which is equipped with a transformer and a heatsink
assembly.
The arrangement of Area 75 is shown in the Linear Accelerator Corrective Maintenance Manual Movement Systems.
For more information on the gantry movement system, see Linear Accelerator Corrective
Maintenance Manual - Movement Systems.
For more information on the motor drive PSUs, see Linear Accelerator Corrective Maintenance
Manual - System Communications.

4.7.2.5 READY indication (optional)
A Ready indication provides a closing contact to allow indication that the linear accelerator is in
the Ready to Start state, with the LT contactors, and movements system contactors enabled.
The Ready lamp uses contacts PL73E-14 and PL73E-15 and relay RL7 on the IRC-74B PCB. The input
is normally open, which allows a client's supply to be used together with a warning lamp. The
warnings in the equipment room and the treatment room indicate the transfer of the machine to
the Ready to Start state.
Relay RL7 on the IRC-74B PCB is energized from the contacts of relay RLA2 on the ROC-ICB PCB by a
signal from a programmable logic device (PLD) on the DIE-ICB PCB. The PLD is activated when item
i495 (Global State ICB) is received.
4.7.2.6 Radiation warning lamp
The radiation warning lamp output circuit is powered whenever the HT system is energized. The
circuit uses contacts on primary HT1 contactor CON-J, the secondary HT2 contactor CON-K and the
HT soft start contactor CON-D to supply power to the RADIATION ON or RADIATION OFF warning
lamps.
The RADIATION ON warning lamp is illuminated when:
CON-D is energized
or
CON-J and CON-K are energized.
The RADIATION OFF warning lamp is illuminated when
CON-D and CON-J are de-energized
or
CON-D and CON-K are de-energized.
The supply for the lamps is provided by the client.
4.7.2.7 Room lights
The level of intensity of the room lights is controlled by relay RL6 on the IRC-74B PCB. The relay
contacts are connected to:
PL73E-18 - normally open
PL73E-19 - common
PL73E-20 - normally closed
The contacts route the full power to the room lights, or supply the room lights through a dimmer
switch.
Relay RL6 on the IRC-74B PCB is energized by transistor TR5 on the ROC-ICB PCB when item i325
(Lights dim) is received. Item i325 is generated in response to i13 (Light request), which is
generated when the ROOM LIGHTS key on the HHC is pressed.

5.1.3 Dosimetry performance data
5.1.3.1 Type
Dual-channel dose monitoring system that uses independent ionization chambers. The two
channels are designated channel A and channel B.
5.1.3.2 Definition of monitor units
1 monitor unit (MU) is approximately equal to 1cGy.
5.1.3.3 Normal termination
The set dose equals the dose delivered in segment MUs in channel A.
5.1.3.4 Abnormal terminations
An abnormal termination occurs when:
• The dose monitored by channel B exceeds the set dose by 10MU.
• The doses monitored by channel A and channel B differ by more than 2MU or 2%,
whichever is the greater.
• The preset treatment time has elapsed.
• The set value of beam MUs is reached.
• The channel A dose rate exceeds 1200MU/minute (25% greater than nominal, for slow
excursions).
• The absorbed dose-rate at the normal treatment distance is greater than 125% or less
than 75% of the nominal value over a period of 5 seconds. In this event, a software dose
rate interlock terminates irradiation.
5.1.3.5 Reproducibility ()
Better than ±0.5% for electron and X-ray modes.
5.1.3.6 Proportionality
In a series of irradiations in the range of 50MU/minute to the maximum dose rate, and for doses
distributed over the range 50MU to 1000MU, the proportionality of an accumulated dose as
measured by an external dosemeter at the isocenter) is within ±1% or 1 MU, whichever is greater.
5.1.3.7 Linearity
The proportionality specification given in Section5.1.3.6 applies to the normal range of preset
dose rates. Under these conditions, the linear accelerator delivers a constant calibrated dose per
pulse.
Under fault conditions it may be possible to achieve a variable dose per pulse. The condition can
be simulated by selecting manual gun in Service Mode, when the delivered dose error will not
exceed ±5% of the indicated dose for dose rates up to twice the specified maximum.
5.1.3.8 Dependence on position of linear accelerator assembly
For any angle of gantry or BLD, the precision of the dosimetry system is ±1% or 1MU, whichever is
greater.

Accessories
5.7 Accessories
5.7.1 Loading conditions
WARNING5.1
Do not attach end frames with a weight of more than 7 kg. If you ignore this
warning, it can cause fatal injury, clinical mistreatment, or damage to the
equipment.
WARNING5.2
Do not put more than 30 kg of shielding blocks on to a shadow tray for gantry
angles of 0° or 180°. For all other gantry angles, do not put more than 15 kg of
shielding blocks on to a shadow tray. If you ignore this warning, it can cause fatal
injury or damage to the equipment.
WARNING5.3
Make sure that you only use the accessories attached to the BLD in their safe work
limits. If you ignore this warning, it can cause fatal injury, clinical mistreatment, or
damage to the equipment.
The conditions for safe work limits for accessories attached to the BLD are:
1 A force greater than 250N must not be applied on the hook or latch on the accessory ring.
2 Accessories must weigh less than 50kg.
3 The center of mass of an accessory must not be more than 80mm from the BLD accessory
ring.
5.7.2 BLD accessories
5.7.2.1 Field defining system
The optical projection system with an indication of the field center by crosswires and wedge filter
orientation. The system maintains an accuracy of 1mm at 100cm and 2mm at floor level.
5.7.2.2 Distance meter
Optical distance meter which projects a scale to indicate the SSD over the range 75cm to 170cm
(accuracy ±3mm).
5.7.2.3 Touchguard
A guard ring fitted around the BLD aperture, which inhibits movements if the ring touches
anything in the path of the moving BLD.
It should be noted that the BLD is effectively extended when a shadow tray is fitted and therefore
the touchguard no longer provides touch protection.

Introduction
Document scope
1.1 Document scope
The corrective maintenance manual (CMM) helps service engineers troubleshoot, repair and
maintain the systems, subsystems and components of the linear accelerator. The target audience
is qualified service engineers. These may be engineers employed directly by Elekta, qualified
representatives of Elekta or qualified representatives of Elekta's customers.
The manual provides:
• A description of the system or sub-system in question.
• A troubleshooting section to identify the problem areas.
• A set of detailed procedures used to replace FRUs (field replaceable units).
• A section on how to return the device to work.
If you find any mistakes in this document, or identify areas for improvement, please raise a CLM
(customer lifecycle management) case and assign it to the relevant queue.

General safety information
Important safety instructions
2.1 Important safety instructions
It is important to install, operate, maintain, and dispose of the equipment according to the
information in the product documentation, and in compliance with local regulations. For the
safety of the users and the patients, before a user operates or works on the equipment, they
must read, understand, and obey all:
• Warnings, cautions, instructions, and notes in this document and the related
documents.
• Safety instructions, emergency procedures, and information in this document and the
related documents.
• Warnings, cautions, and safety markings on the equipment and the accessories of the
equipment.
If you have local work instructions for the equipment, then Elekta recommends that you include
the warnings, cautions, and notes from this document in your local work instructions.
2.1.1 Conventions for warnings, cautions, and notes
The conventions give information about the class and the level of the risk in the warnings and
cautions, and the content of notes.
WARNING 2.1
A warning is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions with a risk of fatal or serious
injury, injury, or clinical mistreatment, if you do not obey the instructions.
CAUTION 2.1
A caution is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions with a risk of damage to the
equipment, data, or the environment, if you do not obey the instructions.
Note: A note gives more information about a related text.
2.1.2 Expected service life of the equipment
The expected service life is the length of time that the regular service and repair procedures can
keep the equipment safe to operate.
WARNING 2.2
Do not operate the equipment unless you correctly complete the safety checks, planned
maintenance schedules, and extended life checks. If you ignore this warning, you can cause
fatal injury and damage to the equipment.
The expected service life of this equipment is 15 years of normal use.
The Elekta definition for 'expected service life' is the length of time that the regular service and
repair procedures can keep the equipment safe to operate.
The Elekta definition of 'normal use' is the treatment of 50 patients each day for five days each
week of the year. If the equipment is used more frequently than this, the frequency of the
planned maintenance must increase accordingly and the extended life checks must also be
brought forward accordingly.

General safety information
Important safety instructions
The level of operation of the equipment can be different to ‘normal use’. This has an effect on the
length of the service life. Because of wear of parts, the risk of a malfunction can increase after 10
years operation. Elekta recommends that before you continue operation after 10 years, you
complete the regular extended life checks.
Elekta can help the User with the correct safety checks, planned maintenance schedules, and the
regular extended life checks for continued safe operation of the equipment.
The system must be maintained throughout its expected service life in compliance with the EMC
information detailed in the applicable Instructions for Use.
For information on the above checks and schedules, contact your local Elekta representative.

2.2.14 Safety precaution for the removal of parts from the radiation head
WARNING 2.21
Do not touch the flight tube, bending magnet, or other parts near to them until a check for

ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury.

become radioactive and a radiation hazard. Before you do work on, or remove parts from the
radiation head, use a calibrated radiation detector to measure the level of induced radioactivity.
Use the applicable safety procedures when you remove radioactive parts and material. The
maximum dose rate for the safe removal of radioactive parts and material is 50 µSv/hr
(microsievert per hour). Do not remove the radioactive parts and material from the treatment
room before they are correctly prepared for safe removal.

Safety precautions
2.2.16.1 Safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity
The safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity are the necessary safety
precautions to know to prevent excessive exposure to radioactivity, which can cause serious
injury or damage to the environment.
Always use two radiation detectors to measure the level of induced radioactivity. Only use
radiation detectors that have an applicable calibration certificate. The period of time since the
last calibration date must be less than 12 months. Do not use the radiation detectors if the period
of time since the last calibration date is more than 12 months.
WARNING 2.23
Do not move radioactive material (by air, sea, or land) unless you obey the applicable laws and
regulations for induced radioactivity and disposal of radioactive material of the jurisdictions
through which the movement occurs. If you ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury
and damage to the environment.
2.2.16.2 Safety precautions for handling parts with induced radioactivity
The handling of parts with induced radioactivity must comply with the laws and regulations of the
jurisdiction in which the equipment is installed. The safe levels of radiation applicable in the UK
do not apply in all jurisdictions. The permitted level of radioactivity must always be as low as
reasonably achievable (ALARA). This level may vary depending on local rules, therefore the safe
working levels from the applicable local rules must be considered as the acceptable working limit.
If there are no safe levels available for a jurisdiction, use the UK value as a guideline, which is a
maximum of 150 cps at the surface for a maximum duration of 72 minutes. The following table
shows the conversion from this value to other units.

Regulatory requirements for equipment use
CAUTION 3.2
Do not touch the parts identified with the ESD caution label. Always obey the ESD precautions
during work on these parts. If you ignore this caution, you can cause damage to the equipment.
Semiconductor devices, integrated circuits, and the parts that contain them, are ESD sensitive
devices. These devices are electrostatic discharge sensitive (ESDS) devices. ESD can cause damage
to these devices and cause them to have a malfunction immediately or some time after the

Product description
Cooling water, gas and vacuum systems on the linear accelerator
4.1 Cooling water, gas and vacuum systems on the linear
accelerator
The linear accelerator has internal and external cooling water systems to keep high temperature
parts of the linear accelerator at a specified temperature.
The internal cooling water system has a water pump that moves distilled water around the system
to remove the heat from the high temperature parts. The warm distilled water flows through the
heat exchanger on the cooling water unit, where the temperature decreases before it moves back
around the system. The heat exchanger is also connected to the external water system, where
cold water from the hospital water supply or a water chiller moves through the heat exchanger to
cool the water in the internal water system. The warm water in the external water system flows
from the heat exchanger to the hospital drain or to the input of the water chiller.
The capacity of the internal cooling water system is 18 L (4 UK gallons, 4.8 US gallons), but
approximately 25 L (5.5 UK gallons, 6.6 US gallons) are necessary to fill and bleed the system.
The rectangular waveguide on the linear accelerator contains the dielectric gas. The dielectric gas
keeps the waveguide cool and prevents high voltage discharge. An external gas cylinder with a gas
regulator supplies the dielectric gas to a valve in AREA 60 or on the RIC. The TCS can open the
valve when the linear accelerator starts and automatically fill the waveguide with the dielectric
gas. If the gas pressure is too high, the pressure release valve that is set at 1.5 bar prevents
damage to the waveguide. The valve is set at the factory or when the linear accelerator is
installed.
The linear accelerator waveguide is evacuated to a specified vacuum. This prevents collisions
between electrons and gas molecules that can cause the electrons to change direction or stop. To
evacuate to the specified vacuum, the waveguide is first evacuated with the use of a rotary vane
pump or a turbomolecular pump. For the linear accelerators with the Varian ion pumps, Elekta
recommends that you use the turbomolecular pump to evacuate the waveguide, because this
pump makes a better vacuum. When the waveguide is at the correct vacuum, two ion pumps
keep the vacuum at the specified level for the correct operation of the linear accelerator. One of
the ion pumps is at the target end of the waveguide and the second ion pump is at the gun end.
The vacuum pressure at the gun end and target end of the waveguide is displayed on the screen
displays in the control room and the treatment room.
The TCS uses the software items to monitor and control the cooling water, gas and vacuum
systems.
4.2 Cooling water system
4.2.1 Description of the external cooling water system
The function of the external cooling water system is to:
• Supply the cold water to the heat exchanger on the cooling water unit from the
primary water supply of the hospital or the water chiller.
• Send the warm water from the heat exchanger to the drain system of the hospital or
the inlet of the water chiller.
Most of the parts of the external cooling water circuit are in the cable reeling post (AREA 60) or
the RIC in the equipment room.

Product description
Cooling water system
4.2.1.1 Description of the external cooling water inlet
The inlet of the external cooling water supply is connected to the external cooling water system at
the cable reeling post or the RIC.
The inlet side of the external cooling water system has:
• A manual stop valve to isolate the external cooling water supply during maintenance.
• A coarse strainer to keep out unwanted material.
• A pressure gauge to show the pressure of the external cooling water supply.
• A connection to the external inlet side of the heat exchanger on the cooling water unit.
4.2.1.2 Description of the external cooling water outlet
The outlet side of the external cooling water system has:
• A connection from the external outlet side of the heat exchanger to a three-way valve
with a motor or actuator control.
Note: The three-way valve increases or decreases the cold water flow through the heat exchanger to
control the water temperature of the internal cooling water system.
• A pressure gauge that shows the outlet pressure of the water from external cooling
water system.
• A 1 bar (15 psi) pressure release valve between the inlet and outlet pipes of the
external cooling water supply.
Note: The pressure release valve changes the direction of the flow of the external water supply when the
three-way valve is closed.
• A manual stop valve to isolate the external cooling water system during maintenance.
• A connection from the manual stop valve to the external cooling supply.
If the external cooling water supply is from the hospital primary water supply, the outlet connects
to the hospital drain system. If the external cooling water supply is from a water chiller, the outlet
connects to the inlet of the water chiller.
4.2.2 Internal cooling water system
The internal cooling water system is a closed loop, pressurized system that contains distilled
water. It has a primary supply circuit and a number of smaller circuits that go to different parts of
the linear accelerator. The distilled water removes heat from the high temperature parts of the
linear accelerator and then flows through the heat exchanger on the cooling water unit. In the
heat exchanger, heat transfers from the distilled water to the water in the external water system.
The pipes of the internal water system have a layer of the chemical benzotriazole on the inner
part of the pipes. This prevents the growth of microorganisms. The benzotriazole is installed at
the factory and stays active for the life of the linear accelerator.
An electric pump in AREA 60 or on the RIC fills the internal cooling water system with distilled
water from a container. As the internal cooling water system fills with water, it is necessary to
bleed the air out of the system. The bleed valves are on the cooling water unit and the digital
accelerator. It is important to remove as much air as possible for correct operation of the cooling
water system.

4.2.3 Control of the cooling water system
4.2.3.1 Description and operation of the control circuit of the internal cooling water
system
The water pressure in the internal cooling water system can change during the operation of the
digital accelerator. The expansion vessel absorbs small changes, which do not stop the operation
of the cooling water system or the digital accelerator.
If a fault occurs or air gets in the system, there can be a large change in the pressure. The control
circuit operates two low pressure switches and one high pressure switch. The switches cause an
inhibit when a fault occurs which stops the operation of the water pump and the digital
accelerator.
The high pressure switch (SW41-2) opens when the pressure increases to more than 1 bar
(14.5 psi). Software item i197 of the TCS senses this and stops the HT. This inhibit appears in the
inhibit list of the TCS.
The first low pressure switch (SW41-3) opens when the water pressure decreases to less than
0.5 bar (7.25 psi). Software item i196 of the TCS senses this and stops the HT. This inhibit appears
in the inhibit list of the TCS.
If the water pressure decreases to less than 0.2 bar (2.9 psi), the second low pressure switch
(SW41-1) opens and de-energizes the primary system contactor CON-A.
4.2.3.2 Description of the flow switches in the cooling water system of linear
accelerators to 152177
The cooling water system has four flow switches that monitor the flow of the cooling water
through the:
• Waveguide injector to the magnetron.
• Waveguide relativistic section to the:
– Focus coils
– RF load, charge transformer, pulse transformer, magnetron magnet, and RF
isolator
– Target flight tube.
The flow switches measure the difference in pressure as the water flows through a calibrated hole
in the flow switch. The difference in pressure operates a flexible diaphragm that controls a
microswitch. When the water flow rate decreases, the pressure in the flow switch also decreases.
If the pressure in the flow switch goes below the calibrated setting, the microswitch gives a
warning of low water flow rate.
The flow switches operate the LT interlock circuit. When the flow rate is below the calibrated
setting, the flow switch operates and switches off the LT supply. An inhibit is displayed on the TCS.
For example, the calibration of the flow switch in the waveguide injector and magnetron water
system is set to measure a pressure decrease of 0.14 bar (2 psi) at a flow rate of 18 L/min (3.96
UK gallons/min, 4.76 US gallons/min).

• Waveguide injector to the magnetron.
• Waveguide relativistic section to the target flight tube.
The flow switches have a sensor that hangs in the water flow. When the water flow rate is above
the calibrated setting, the sensor moves and closes a magnetic switch. When the water flow rate
is below the calibrated setting, the sensor moves back to the start position and opens the switch.
The flow switches operate the LT interlock circuit. When the water flow rate is below the
calibrated setting, the switch opens. This switches off the LT supply and displays an inhibit on the
TCS. For example, the calibration of the flow switch in the waveguide injector and magnetron
water system is set to measure a pressure decrease of 0.14 bar (2 psi) at a flow rate of 18 L/min
(3.96 UK gallons/min, 4.76 US gallons/min).
The safe condition is a water flow rate that is approximately 25% above the water flow rate at
which the switch operates. For example, if the switch operates at 22.5 L/min (4.95 UK gallons/
min, 5.94 US gallon/min), the safe water flow rate is 27 L/min (5.94 UK gallons/min, 7.13 US
gallons/min).
Do not adjust the settings of the flow switches. The parameters of operation for the flow switches
are set by the manufacturer. If you change the settings of the flow switches, an incorrect
indication of the safe flow rate of the cooling water can occur.
4.2.3.4 Description of the three-way valve and actuator for linear accelerators from
serial number 152178
The three-way valve has two inputs A and B, and one output AB. Water in the external water
circuit flows directly to the A input of the valve. Water in the external water circuit that flows
through the heat exchanger goes to the B input of the valve. Water from the AB output flows to
the outlet of the external water circuit.
The temperature controller monitors the temperature of the internal water circuit with a K-type
thermocouple attached to the supply manifold. If the temperature increases, the controller
operates the actuator to open the B to AB path. This increases the flow of water through the heat
exchanger from the external water circuit. If the temperature decreases, the controller decreases
the flow of cool water through the B to AB path. If the temperature decreases sufficiently, the
controller fully closes the B to AB path. The cool water then flows through the A to AB path and
bypasses the heat exchanger.
4.2.3.5 Description of the temperature controller of linear accelerators from serial
number 152178 to 152971
The temperature controller is a rectangular device and is installed on the cooling water unit. Wire
connections for the power supply, thermocouple and actuator are made to terminals at the
bottom of the controller. There are two LCDs on the top that display actual temperature and set
temperature. The 24 VDC power supply to the controller comes from the UMD (AREA 11).

4.2.3.7 Description of the water temperature control for linear accelerators to serial
number 152177
When the linear accelerator starts, water flows through the internal cooling water system. To help
increase the temperature of the water, the TCS null calibration block applies a current to the
bending magnet and focus coils. Usually, the internal cooling water temperature is set to 30°C.
As distilled water flows through the internal water system, a temperature sensor diode in the
supply manifold measures the water temperature. The forward voltage decrease of the
temperature sensor diode changes at the rate of 2 mV/°C. The system reads the sensor output
continuously and sends it to the TCS where it is displayed as i223.
Signals derived from the voltage of the temperature sensor diode open or close the three-way
valve in the external cooling water system to keep the necessary temperature. The three-way
valve controls the flow of water through the heat exchanger, which controls the temperature of
the water in the internal water system to ±1°C.
If the water temperature is more than 42°C, a high temperature switch on the supply manifold
opens to disconnect the electrical supply. This switch is part of the interlock chain that includes
the low water pressure and water pump temperature.
4.2.3.8 Description of the water temperature control for linear accelerators 152178 to
152971
When the linear accelerator starts, the distilled water that flows through the internal cooling
water system increases in temperature. To help increase the temperature, the TCS null calibration
block applies a current to the bending magnet and focus coils.
As distilled water flows through the internal cooling water system, a temperature sensor diode in
the supply manifold measures the water temperature. The forward voltage decrease of the
temperature sensor diode changes at the rate of 2 mV/°C. The output of the sensor is read
continuously and sent to the treatment control system (TCS) where it is displayed as i223.
Usually, the internal cooling water temperature is set to 28 °C. The linear accelerator uses a
temperature controller on the cooling water unit to control the temperature of the distilled water.
The controller uses a K-type thermocouple on the supply manifold to measure the temperature of
the internal cooling water. To adjust the temperature, it operates an actuator attached to a threeway valve that controls the flow of cool water from the external water system through the heat
exchanger.
If the water temperature increases to 35 °C, a high temperature software interlock operates.
If the water temperature is more than 42 °C, a high temperature switch on the supply manifold
opens and disconnects the electrical supply. This switch is part of the interlock chain that includes
the switches for the low water pressure and the water pump temperature.

4.2.3.9 Description of the water temperature control for linear accelerators from

The TCS reads the output continuously and displays it on the TCS as i223. The TCS continues to

4.3 Description of the dielectric gas system
The dielectric gas prevents HT discharge when the RF travels through the parts of the rectangular
waveguide that do not have a vacuum.
When the linear accelerator starts, the TCS opens a top-up valve for approximately two minutes.
This lets dielectric gas from the dielectric gas cylinder fill the gas system. A pressure switch on the
cable reeling post or the RIC closes the valve automatically when the pressure is more than
1.0 bar.
A manual valve is installed in line with the supply from the gas regulator. During maintenance
tasks, the manual valve can be closed to isolate the gas cylinder. You can close the valve to
prevent the automatic operation of the gas supply when the machine state changes to Closed.
4.3.1 Description of the dielectric gas sulfur hexafluoride
Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) is a greenhouse gas. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change
(IPCC) identified SF6 gas as the most dangerous greenhouse gas. During a 100 year period, it is
possible that SF6 gas can warm the environment 22,200 times more than CO2.
You must collect and discard the SF6 gas correctly. It is the responsibility of the user to minimize
the effects on the environment as follows:
• Repair SF6 gas leaks promptly.
• Obey the local regulations to collect and discard the unwanted SF6 gas.

4.3.2 Description of the preferential breakdown (disassociation) of the
dielectric gas sulfur hexafluoride
The material that absorbs power in the high power RF load of the digital accelerator can be
damaged. If this occurs, it can cause preferential breakdown (disassociation) of the dielectric gas
in the rectangular waveguide.
Disassociation occurs in water vapor or oxygen. It is then possible to make sulfur decafluoride
(S2F10) but only when there are applicable percentages of oxygen and SF6.
The products of disassociation in water vapor and oxygen are as follows:
• Thionyl fluoride (SOF2)
• Sulfuryl fluoride (SO2F2)
• Thionyl tetrafluoride (SOF4).
More chemical reactions can occur in water vapor. These types of chemical reaction makes weak
concentrations of hydrochloric and hydrofluoric acids.
Do not smoke cigarettes near the SF6 gas, because it can cause disassociation of the SF6
molecules. This type of disassociation can cause a toxic mixture of gases in the air that have a
strong smell. If this occurs, go out of the room immediately, and use a pump to evacuate the
room until the room does not smell.
4.3.3 Description of the dielectric gas cylinder for linear accelerators to
152783
The dielectric gas cylinder holds the dielectric gas for the waveguide system on the linear
accelerator. The gas cylinder is installed in the cable reeling post (AREA 60), or installed on a wall
near the cable reeling post and held in position by brackets and chain straps.
Note: A gas cylinder with a maximum size of 1460 mm × 230 mm can be installed in the cable reeling

A multistage gas regulator is installed to the outlet of the gas cylinder. An inlet connection kit,
supplied with the linear accelerator, can connect the gas regulator to different gas cylinder outlets
in different countries. The inlet pressure is 4.83 bar (70 psi) and the preset outlet pressure is
0.8 ±0.05 bar (12 ±0.75 psi).

4.3.5 Description of the dielectric gas top-up valve
The top-up valve opens and closes at regular intervals to keep the correct quantity of dielectric
gas in the rectangular waveguide. It also isolates the dielectric gas cylinder from the waveguide
when the digital accelerator is off during the system start cycle.
The top-up valve connects to the dielectric gas cylinder and the rectangular waveguide. For digital
accelerators to serial number 152783, the valve is in the cable reeling post (AREA 60). For digital
accelerators from serial number 152784, the valve is in the RIC.
When software item i336 (top-up gas) is set to 1 in Service Mode, the treatment control system
(TCS) automatically controls the operation of the top-up valve. The TCS opens the top-up valve
when the machine state changes to Closed. A pressure switch closes the top-up valve
automatically if the gas pressure increases to more than 1 bar.
4.3.6 Description of the pressure indication for the dielectric gas system
The pressure gauge shows the current gas pressure and the minimum permitted gas pressure in
the waveguide. The pressure release valve prevents the buildup of too much pressure in the
waveguide which can cause damage to the waveguide. The pressure switch stops the radiation
delivery if the waveguide pressure is not in the defined limits for safe operation.
The pressure gauge and pressure switch assembly, and the pressure release valve are installed in
AREA 22 of the gantry. The pressure release valve is installed adjacent to pressure gauge and
pressure switch assembly on the gantry drum, between the gantry drum and the modulator
assembly.
The pressure gauge measures the gas pressure in bar. The black pointer shows the gas pressure in
the waveguide, which is approximately 0.8 bar. The red pointer is set to the minimum permitted
pressure, which is usually 0.7 bar. This sets the operation points of the pressure switch.
The pressure switch is connected to the TCS as software item i243 (gas pressure). The connection
is through the IRC-B PCB on the gantry drum (AREA 14), and DIE-HTB PCB in the HTCA (AREA 16).
The TCS monitors i243 (gas pressure) and stops radiation if the switch opens.
The control knob on the pressure release valve sets the pressure at which the valve operates. A
center screw locks the control knob at a pressure setting of 1.5 bar (21.8 psi).
4.3.7 Description of the dielectric gas extraction pump
The dielectric gas extraction pump installed on the gantry drum (AREA 15) is a vacuum pump.
Before maintenance, use the dielectric gas extraction pump to evacuate the air, water vapor, and
dielectric gas from the waveguide system.
4.3.8 Operation of the control circuit of the dielectric gas system
When the digital accelerator is energized, the TCS sends i336 (top-up gas) to the ROC-ICA PCB.
This energizes relay RL7 on the IRC-C PCB. This completes the interlock circuit from interlock
transformer T2 to the coil of the dielectric gas valve (SW60A) on the cable reeling post or RIC. At
the same time, the TCS starts a 15 minute timeout counter to let the gas pressure increase and
operate the pressure switch (SW60B), which closes the valve (SW60A). If the gas pressure is too
low to operate the pressure switch (SW60B) in the timeout period, the TCS de-energizes the valve
to isolate the gas cylinder. The cause can be an empty gas cylinder or a gas leak.
The pressure gauge (AREA 22) also monitors the gas pressure. It has a minimum level switch that
is usually set to operate at 0.7 bar. The HT cannot be switched on until the pressure of the
dielectric gas increases to the necessary minimum pressure. This is because the FPLA on the DIEHTB PCB that monitors the pressure gauge switch is part of the HT/PRF interlock chain.
